request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: The Keplerian ellipse fails badly: the residual RMS is about 108,000 arcsec (~30 deg), and the noise sigma was fitted to that RMS, so rms/sigma = 1 says nothing about fit quality. The residuals show strong systematic east-west trends against both time and heliocentric distance. Splitting the arc in two gives very different periods (4125 vs 11990 days) and an apsidal shift of about 96 deg per orbit. Strong apsidal precession together with an inconsistent period-distance relation points to a central force that departs from pure inverse-square. North residuals are small, so the motion stays planar and a central-force explanation fits. An unseen perturber cannot plausibly produce 96 deg per orbit of precession. The first step is to try the registered integrated central-force families, which differ in how the deviation scales with r.

proposals.rationale: A free exponent n and strength C give a general power-law departure from 1/r^2. This yields apsidal precession and a modified period-distance scaling with just one extra parameter beyond Kepler.
Adding an inverse-cube correction is the classic cause of steady apsidal precession. With fixed GM this tests whether a 1/r^3 term explains the 96 deg/orbit shift.

A screened force weakens at large r, which would lengthen the effective period at the far end of the orbit. That matches the much longer period fitted to the second half, when the body was at 10-11 AU.
